newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Berlusconi offers Europe-welfare deal.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Berlusconi offers Europe-welfare deal.

text.p: Centre-right opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi on Thursday offered a deal with the government on reforming the welfare state to boost Italy's EMU hopes and warned Prime Minister Romano Prodi not to "play with fire".

Berlusconi, in a letter to leftist newspaper L'Unita, proposed striking "a transparent compromise" with the government and establishing an "understanding for Europe" to help meet the EMU commitments while reforming Italy's welfare state.

"The turbulence of the lira against the mark and the dollar are just a first sign, a taste of what could happen if the prospect of Italian membership of the European single currency club should enter a crisis," Berlusconi wrote.

"We now need to see whether it would not be opportune, on the delicate and undelayable issue of reform of some aspects of the welfare state, to reach an understanding for Europe based on the absolute exclusion of new taxes and the necessary determination to reduce...unproductive social spending."

Berlusconi said the Prodi's centre-left government, which on Wednesday announced it was drawing up a mini-budget to ensure it would be ready for European economic and monetary union in 1999, had earlier "wisely" suggested bringing forward the 1998 budget.
"We repeat very strongly, with no ulterior motives...that a transparent, open deal on welfare spending cannot be delayed," he said.
Berlusconi said he hoped his proposal would be supported by the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), the biggest party in government, which was opening a four-day congress on Thursday.

"You mustn't play with fire if you're a responsible politician," Berlusconi wrote. "And not understanding that the economy needs, in view of Europe, a bipartisan accord on reform of the welfare state, that indeed means playing with fire."

Gianfranco Fini, leader of the far-right National Alliance and Berlusconi's main ally, said on Wednesday that the government could "forget about" support from the centre-right Freedom Alliance for the mini-budget if it included new taxes.
But he said that an early 1998 budget would be a different matter.
Prodi has yet to announce the size of the mini-budget, which comes hard on the heels of a 1997 budget designed to chop 62.5 trillion lire ($37.2 billion) off this year's deficit.

The need for a mini-budget, which the market expects to include some 13-15 trillion lire of deficit-cutting measures, became plain after Italy overshot its deficit target. ($1=1,679) -- Rome newsroom +396 678 2501
